strengths: Principled and intuitive formulation: Decomposing the representation-matching cost into grouping error (clustering/matching) and approximation error (weight retrofitting) provides a clear theoretical lens for model merging.

Theoretical grounding: Theorem 1 proves the exactness of the error decomposition via importance-weighted centroids, and Theorem 2 provides concrete optimality and approximation guarantees for Hungarian and K-means fusion in linear settings.

Strong performance in challenging regimes: The method achieves substantial gains in zero-shot accuracy under extreme class-sharded and non-IID distributions where existing weight-averaging baselines (such as activation-based Git Re-Basin and OTFusion) collapse to near-random performance.

Broad architectural flexibility: Demonstrated empirical validity across multiple distinct architectures (VGGs, ResNets, and Vision Transformers), various widths/depths, and diverse datasets (CIFAR-10/100, Tiny-ImageNet, BloodMNIST, and ImageNet-1k).

Thorough experimental reporting: The paper includes runtime analysis, landscape visualizations, ablations on fusion dataset size, and extensive appendix tables reporting standard deviations across multiple random seeds.
weaknesses: Reliance on calibration/fusion data: The method requires a forward pass over a dataset to extract activations and (for the gradient variants) multiple optimization epochs per layer. While common in activation-based fusion, this requires data access that pure weight-space merging methods do not.

Gap between theory and practical clustering: The approximation guarantee in Theorem 2(b) assumes the local-search algorithm of Kanungo et al. (2002), whereas the practical implementation uses Lloyd's algorithm with k-means++.

Variable impact of neuron attribution: While the incorporation of attribution scores (Conductance, DeepLIFT) is framed as a primary innovation, in several benchmarks (e.g., Tables 16, 17, 18, and 20) the performance gains over uniform weighting are marginal or fall within experimental error bars.

Computational overhead compared to weight-averaging baselines: Fitting weights via SGD per level (e.g., 100 epochs per level in KF-Gradient) significantly increases fusion latency relative to closed-form or single-pass matching algorithms, though the authors partially justify this against full fine-tuning budgets.

strengths: Principled and intuitive formulation: Decomposing the level-wise representation matching cost into an approximation error and a grouping error (Theorem 1) provides a clean mathematical justification for decoupling clustering/matching from subnetwork parameter fitting.

Strong empirical performance in non-IID and sharded regimes: Prior alignment/weight-matching methods (such as OTFusion and activation-based Git Re-Basin) notoriously collapse to near-random performance under extreme label sharding or non-IID partitions. The proposed retrofitting framework achieves high zero-shot performance (e.g., 54.5% vs. ~2-4% on CIFAR-100 ViT in Table 2, and 88.7% on BloodMNIST in Table 3).

Generality and architectural flexibility: Unlike many prior methods restricted strictly to pairwise fusion of identical architectures, the proposed framework handles multiple models, varying model widths (Table 16), different architectures (VGG, ResNet, ViT), and can be repurposed for model compression (Table 8).

Comprehensive evaluation and transparency: The manuscript includes multiple seeds with standard deviations across diverse benchmarks (CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, Tiny-ImageNet, BloodMNIST, ImageNet-1k subset), detailed runtime breakdowns, and open-source implementation details.
weaknesses: Ambiguity in the 'zero-shot' / 'without retraining' terminology: In the model merging literature, 'zero-shot' or 'training-free' typically refers to direct weight manipulation without gradient descent steps. The gradient-based variants (HF-Gradient and KF-Gradient) run up to 100 epochs of AdamW per level on a fusion dataset (Table 9). While computationally cheaper than full end-to-end retraining, this is essentially a stage-wise distillation / layer-wise regression procedure rather than purely training-free merging.

Marginal empirical benefit from neuron attribution scores in core settings: While the incorporation of saliency scores (Conductance, DeepLIFT) is highlighted as a primary contribution, its empirical advantage over uniform weighting is frequently minimal or within error bars (e.g., in Table 7, Table 17, and Table 18, KF-Gradient with uniform weighting matches or occasionally outperforms Conductance and DeepLIFT).

Discrepancy between theory and practice: While Theorem 1 and Theorem 2 consider importance-weighted approximation loss, Section F.1 notes that in practice, plain unweighted MSE is used during the gradient-based approximation step because weighted MSE yields noisy representations in later layers. This breaks the strict correspondence with the theoretical objective decomposition in Equation (2).

Computational overhead and scalability: Fitting weights iteratively level-by-level using SGD adds significant runtime overhead compared to one-shot permutation algorithms (e.g., taking over 10 minutes on small datasets, as shown in Table 11 and Table 12). Furthermore, experiments remain limited to smaller-scale computer vision benchmarks and have not been demonstrated on modern large-scale architectures or language models.

strengths: Principled and clear formulation: The paper frames model fusion as an intermediate representation-matching problem and neatly decouples the objective into a grouping error (clustering/matching) and an approximation error (weight retrofitting), supported by theoretical guarantees (Theorems 1 and 2).

Generality and architectural flexibility: Unlike many prior methods restricted to pairwise fusion or specific feedforward architectures, the proposed framework naturally accommodates more than two models, models with varying widths/depths, and modern backbones including Vision Transformers and ResNets.

Strong performance under non-IID and sharded regimes: In challenging settings where existing alignment methods (such as OTFusion, Git Re-Basin, and ZipIt!) often collapse to near-random zero-shot accuracy, the proposed HF and KF variants maintain high accuracy and exhibit significant resilience.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: The submission includes extensive experiments across multiple datasets (CIFAR-10/100, Tiny-ImageNet, BloodMNIST, ImageNet-1k), detailed runtime breakdowns, and loss landscape analyses.
weaknesses: Ambiguity surrounding the 'zero-shot' claim: The paper emphasizes zero-shot fusion without retraining, yet the gradient-based variants (HF-Gradient, KF-Gradient) optimize weights level-by-level via backpropagation over many epochs on a fusion dataset. This closely resembles greedy layer-wise knowledge distillation/regression rather than strictly data-free or closed-form weight-merging.

Marginal empirical benefit of neuron attribution scores: Incorporating advanced neuron saliency metrics (Conductance and DeepLIFT) is framed as a major contribution, but experimental results across several benchmarks (e.g., Tables 2, 5, 6, 17, and 18) show that non-uniform scores yield minimal or negligible improvements over uniform weighting, and in some full-dataset runs uniform weighting even performs better.

Dependence on fusion dataset size and compute overhead: The gradient retrofitting procedure exhibits substantial performance degradation when the available calibration/fusion dataset is small (as illustrated in Table 4 for ImageNet-1k) and requires significantly higher runtime than lightweight alignment baselines.

Evaluation scale: Experiments are restricted to relatively small models and datasets (e.g., custom small ViTs, VGG11, ResNet-50 on ImageNet subsets). Evaluating on contemporary foundation models or modern LLMs would strengthen the significance of the findings.

strengths: Principled and clear formulation: Decomposing the layer-wise representation matching objective into an interpretable sum of grouping error (clustering) and approximation error (function fitting) provides an elegant theoretical and practical foundation for model fusion.

Extension beyond pairwise matching: While algorithms like Git Re-Basin and standard OTFusion primarily target pairwise one-to-one matching, the proposed K-means Fusion framework naturally accommodates arbitrary numbers of models and differing layer sizes.

Strong performance in heterogeneous settings: The approach demonstrates marked improvements in zero-shot accuracy over baseline methods (OTFusion, Git Re-Basin, Vanilla Averaging) on challenging non-IID and sharded data partitions across both convolutional (VGG-11) and transformer (ViT) architectures.

Theoretical guarantees: Theorem 1 provides an exact decomposition of the objective, and Theorem 2 connects the linear layer formulation to polynomial-time exact matching (via the Hungarian algorithm) and constant-factor approximation guarantees (via local search for K-means).
weaknesses: Limited evaluation scale: Experiments are restricted to relatively small architectures (VGG-11, small 7-block ViT) on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100. Evaluating on larger datasets (e.g., ImageNet) or modern LLMs would significantly strengthen claims regarding broad applicability to contemporary deep networks.

Marginal empirical impact of neuron attribution: While the paper emphasizes the integration of neuron attribution scores (Conductance, DeepLIFT) as a key conceptual contribution, the empirical results in Tables 11, 12, 14, and 15 show that in many cases, uniform weighting performs competitively or nearly identically to the attribution-weighted variants (e.g., 57.0% vs. 57.1% on ViT 2-way non-IID; 83.2% vs. 83.3% on VGG-11 2-way non-IID).

Sensitivity and complexity of the gradient-based variant: As acknowledged by the authors, the gradient-based method requires significant hyperparameter tuning (e.g., differing optimization schedules, noise scales, and task-specific head weighting heuristics across settings), which limits ease of adoption in practice.

strengths: Principled mathematical formulation: The decomposition of the neuron-aware representation matching objective into grouping error and approximation error (Theorem 1) provides a clear and interpretable conceptual framework for layer-wise neural network fusion.

Strong zero-shot performance under distribution shift: The proposed Hungarian Fusion (HF) and K-means Fusion (KF) algorithms show significant performance advantages over existing zero-shot alignment baselines (such as standard OTFusion and Git Re-Basin) on non-IID and sharded class partitions where prior methods degrade severely.

Methodological versatility: The framework supports both a closed-form least-squares linear variant (with theoretical approximation bounds under affine assumptions) and a gradient-based optimization approach applicable to general differentiable architectures such as Vision Transformers.
Clear writing and transparent discussion of limitations: The paper is well-organized, thoroughly explains implementation details, and openly discusses hyperparameters, runtimes, and limitations.
weaknesses: Limited benchmark scale and model diversity: The experimental validation is restricted to small-scale vision benchmarks (CIFAR-10 with VGG11 and CIFAR-100 with a compact custom ViT). Given that recent model merging research often focuses on larger architectures (e.g., standard ResNet-50, large ViTs on ImageNet, or modern LLMs), the practical scalability and effectiveness of activation-level clustering on larger architectures remain unverified.

Mixed empirical impact of neuron attribution scores: While importance scores show significant improvements in certain configurations (e.g., HF Linear and Git Re-Basin on VGG11 in Table 11), their benefits appear negligible or within standard error bars in several ViT settings (e.g., Table 12 and Table 14, where Uniform, Conductance, and DeepLIFT perform essentially identically). Furthermore, the authors note in Appendix B.2 that importance weights are dropped during the approximation phase due to optimization stability issues.

Confounding heuristics: In Appendix F.1, the authors mention employing a 'Head Weights' heuristic (re-weighting logits by class sample proportions), noting that it improves accuracy. It is unclear whether this logit adjustment was also applied to baseline methods (e.g., OTFusion, Git Re-Basin, Last-layer KD), raising questions about how much of the non-IID gain stems from representation fusion versus classification head calibration.

Computational overhead: The K-means clustering and gradient-based fitting steps introduce substantial computational overhead compared to baseline permutation/OT methods (e.g., Table 6 and Table 7 show runtime increasing from ~1–3s to ~80s for VGG and over 600s for ViT), which may restrict application when fusing wider layers or larger batches.

strengths: Principled mathematical formulation: Theorem 1 provides an exact and intuitive decomposition of the layer-wise representation loss into grouping (clustering) error and approximation (fitting) error, offering a clear conceptual framework for understanding model fusion.

Strong performance in zero-shot non-IID and sharded regimes: The proposed algorithms (Hungarian Linear Fusion and K-means Fusion) significantly outperform prior activation/permutation-based baselines like OTFusion and Git Re-Basin in challenging heterogeneous data partitions on CIFAR datasets.

Architecture generality: The formulation applies naturally to both convolutional architectures (VGG11) and transformer blocks (ViTs) through flexible layer-level grouping, rather than requiring architecture-specific ad-hoc permutation heuristics.

Theoretical guarantees under linear assumptions: Theorem 2 proves polynomial-time optimality for Hungarian Fusion on affine layers and bounded approximation ratio for K-means Fusion using Kanungo et al.'s local search algorithm.
weaknesses: Limited evaluation scale: The experiments are conducted exclusively on small-scale datasets (CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100) using relatively small networks (VGG11 and a 7-block compact ViT). Given the recent rapid progress in model merging and federated learning on large vision backbones and language models, the empirical validation feels dated and insufficient to confirm scalability.

Neuron attribution provides negligible benefit on Transformers: A central claimed innovation is incorporating neuron attribution scores (Conductance, DeepLIFT). However, the results on ViT (Tables 12, 13, and 14) reveal essentially identical performance across Uniform, Conductance, and DeepLIFT scores (e.g., Table 12 4-way split: 51.7% across all three; 6-way split: 45.1% uniform vs. 44.9% DeepLIFT). This directly undermines the generality of the attribution claim for modern architectures.

Discrepancy between theory and practical optimization: While Theorem 1 and Eq. (5) formally optimize an importance-weighted MSE, Section B.2 explicitly notes that 'in practice, we do not minimize the weighted MSE, but rather the plain MSE' because low-importance neurons would otherwise degrade intermediate representations. This creates an unbridged gap between the formal theoretical decomposition and the implemented algorithm.

Reliance on configuration heuristics and potential confounders: In Appendix F.1, the authors mention that the gradient variant relies heavily on 'Setting 2' for multi-client non-IID setups, which keeps weights very close to initialization and relies on target matching at the logits level (akin to KD). Furthermore, the application of 'Head Weights' (re-weighting logits by class distribution seen per client) is a known federated learning post-processing trick; it is unclear whether baselines (OTFusion, Git Re-Basin) were afforded this exact same logit re-weighting advantage.

Missing modern model merging baselines: The comparison is restricted primarily to OTFusion, Git Re-Basin, and standard ensembling. Modern model merging methods tailored to representation alignment or weight-space arithmetic (e.g., RegMean, Fisher Merging) are not benchmarked or discussed in the context of different weight spaces.
